newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia said readying strict law on public protest.
newsitem.headline: Croatia said readying strict law on public protest.

text.p: Croatia is preparing a strict law on public protest in what may be a move to contain any dissent if results of regional elections next month are disputed, the newspaper Novi List reported on Friday. The newspaper said authoritarian President Franjo Tudjman's government began drafting the law after mass protests last November forced it to drop its decision to shut down a popular independent radio station.
Croatia's constitution is democratic, but the ruling nationalist HDZ party effectively dominates key institutions including the bureaucracy, judiciary and media.

HDZ leaders tend to depict opposition as disloyalty but polls show Tudjman's party could lose major cities to rival coalitions in the April 13 communal elections, and some critics have wondered whether he would accept defeat.

In nearby Serbia, President Slobodan Milosevic's refusal to recognise opposition victories in municipal voting triggered 10 weeks of street unrest which ended only when the governing Socialists conceded their losses.
Novi List said Croatia's protest law was being drafted by the Interior Ministry apparently with the expectation of post-election protests.

"By coincidence or not, work on the new law began at about the time of demonstrations in Zagreb concerning Radio 101 and (the start) of Belgrade demonstrations against Milosevic," it said. The Interior Ministry refused comment on the report.
But diplomats who monitor Croatia's record on political freedom to assess its credentials for links to the European Union said they saw no ulterior motive for the reported draft law at this time.

They said Croatia, where anti-government protests have been rare since independence from Yugoslavia in 1991, may well lack clear, comprehensive rules on public gatherings and want to correct the problem.
Novi List said a Draft Law on Peaceful Gatherings and Public Protest envisaged wider police powers and heightened legal responsibility for protest organisers.
It said the law would require municipalities, most of them HDZ-run, to designate sites for protests and adopt rules of conduct for protesters.

Protest organisers would have to provide police in advance with details such as the expected number of protesters, their pattern of movement, security measures and so on. Novi List said the law seemed intended to discourage protest rallies.

Tudjman said recently there were no similarities in Croatia to the situation in Serbia and he would accept any vote result, although he voided an opposition win in Zagreb municipal voting two years ago with his "national security" veto.

Western diplomats saw nothing sinister in a new law on protests, saying Tudjman would not want to handicap Croatia's chances of integration in Europe or anger Croats in cities where the HDZ is least popular, including Zagreb.

"Can you imagine what the consequences for the HDZ would be in Zagreb on April 13 if they tried to clamp down on public dissent? This would be a cause celebre for the opposition. The HDZ is not totally stupid," said one senior envoy.
